challenges.name: what-is-inside-the-image-quiz
challenges.title: What is really inside this image?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from Rice Rocket's images: a Dockerfile that deletes a .env file, and an SBOM checked against a security advisory. Decide whether each statement follows from the evidence.

questions.question:
The api image v2.9.0 was built from this Dockerfile. The project folder contained a .env file with DB_PASSWORD=Pr0d-Rice-2026, and there is no .dockerignore:

FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
RUN rm -f /app/.env
CMD ["python", "-m", "api"]

$ docker run --rm ghcr.io/ricerocket/api:v2.9.0 ls -a /app
.  ..  Dockerfile  api  requirements.txt

Statement: "Even though ls shows no .env in the running container, anyone who pulls api:v2.9.0 can still get the password out of the image."
questions.explanation: True. Layers only add. COPY . . created a layer that contains /app/.env with the password. RUN rm -f /app/.env created a new layer that only records "this path is deleted" (a whiteout), so the container's merged view no longer shows the file - but the COPY layer is unchanged and ships with the image. docker save, or any tool that unpacks layers one by one, gets the file back in seconds; a secret scanner that reads every layer reports it. The misconception is that what a container can see is what the image contains. The fixes: keep .env out of the build context with .dockerignore, use a build secret mount for build-time secrets, and rotate the password, because the image has already been pulled.

questions.question:
A security advisory covers PyYAML versions before 5.4. The dispatch service's requirements.txt pins PyYAML==6.0.2. A scanner generated a CycloneDX SBOM from the image ghcr.io/ricerocket/dispatch:v4.1.0; these are all its PyYAML entries (shortened to name, version and where the package was found):

name     version   purl                     found in
pyyaml   6.0.2     pkg:pypi/pyyaml@6.0.2    /app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/PyYAML-6.0.2.dist-info

Part of docker history for the same image:

COPY build/route-report /usr/local/bin/route-report    18.2MB

route-report is a single-file executable that the team builds with PyInstaller from a script whose own requirements pin PyYAML==5.3.1.

Statement: "Because the SBOM lists only PyYAML 6.0.2, the dispatch image v4.1.0 contains no PyYAML version that the advisory covers."
questions.explanation: False. An SBOM lists what the scanner could recognise, mostly from package metadata such as the .dist-info folders pip writes. PyInstaller packs the script, the Python runtime and its libraries (here PyYAML 5.3.1) into one executable, without those folders on the image's filesystem, so a scanner may not list them at all. The image still ships the old PyYAML inside /usr/local/bin/route-report. An entry missing from an SBOM is not proof that the package is absent: check how binaries copied in with COPY were built, generate an SBOM for them when you build them, or rebuild the tool with a fixed PyYAML. The misconception is that the SBOM is a complete inventory by definition.

challenges.name: scan-image-layers-for-secrets
challenges.title: Find the secrets that every layer still carries
challenges.description: Rice Rocket's api image v2.9.0 copied a .env file with the production database password and deleted it in the next step, so docker run ... ls shows nothing - but the file is still inside the earlier layer. Write scan_image(layers), the secret scanner the CI will run on every image before it is pushed. It gets the layers in build order, each with the files it adds (path -> text, or null for a binary file) and the paths it deletes. Check every line of every text file in every layer against the three rules in the starter (an AWS access key id, a private key header, and a NAME=value line whose name contains SECRET, PASSWORD or TOKEN with a real value, not empty and not a $reference). For each finding, report the 1-based layer, the path, the line number, the rule, and in_final_image: false when a later layer deleted that path (or a directory above it) or replaced it with a newer file. Return {"findings": [...], "total": n, "hidden": number not in the final image}, ordered by layer, path, line and rule. The exact rules and an example are in the docstring of scanner.py; the runner at the bottom (do not change it) reads {"layers": [...]} from stdin and prints the result as JSON. Never print the secret itself.
hints: Which question does the scanner answer: "what can a running container see?" or "what bytes does anyone who pulls the image get?" Which layers, and which files, does the second question include?

Split the work into three small functions, as the starter does: rules_for_line(line) looks at one line only; in_final_image(path, index, layers) only looks at the layers after index (their files and their deleted paths, with inside() for directories); scan_image loops over layers, sorted paths and str.splitlines() lines and builds the findings.

A similar case on different data: layers [{"files": {"etc/app.conf": "MAIL_TOKEN=abc"}}, {"deleted": ["etc/"]}]. ASSIGNMENT.fullmatch("MAIL_TOKEN=abc") gives the groups "MAIL_TOKEN" and "abc"; "TOKEN" is in the name and "abc" is a real value, so the line matches secret-assignment. inside("etc/app.conf", "etc/") is True, so the finding is {"layer": 1, "path": "etc/app.conf", "line": 1, "rule": "secret-assignment", "in_final_image": false}, and hidden is 1.

tests.name: The incident: .env copied in layer 2 and removed in layer 3 is still found
